In the landmark Miranda v. Arizona case decided in 1966, the Supreme Court established important protections for individuals in custody. The Court held that law enforcement must inform suspects of their constitutional rights before custodial interrogation. This decision fundamentally changed how police conduct interviews and investigations across the United States. The Miranda rights, commonly known as Miranda warnings, include the right to remain silent, that anything said can be used in court, the right to an attorney, and the right to a court-appointed attorney if unable to afford one. The case arose from the conviction of Ernesto Miranda based on his confession to police. The Court found that his confession was inadmissible because he had not been informed of his rights. This decision has had lasting impacts on criminal procedure and continues to be cited in cases today.
